text:
This is a line chart showing validation loss over training steps for three training methods.

The x-axis is labeled Training step, running from 0 to 10,000 and it starts at zero. The y-axis is labeled Cross-entropy loss, running from about 1.5 to 4.5, and it does not start at zero. There is one panel.

The legend has three series: Baseline in blue, plus LoRA in orange, and Full fine-tune in green.

At step 0, all three start at about 4.5. Around 2,000 steps, all are near 2.7, with Baseline slightly above the others. Around 4,000 steps, Baseline is about 2.25, plus LoRA about 2.12, and Full fine-tune about 2.05. Around 6,000 steps, Baseline is about 2.15, plus LoRA about 1.93, and Full fine-tune about 1.80. At 10,000 steps, Baseline ends near 2.08, plus LoRA near 1.85, and Full fine-tune near 1.62. The lowest visible value is the Full fine-tune curve at the end, about 1.62.

The main pattern is that all three losses fall quickly at first and then flatten out. Full fine-tune performs best throughout most of training, plus LoRA is in the middle, and Baseline is highest. The curves are close early on, then separate more clearly after about 3,000 to 4,000 steps.

This is a bar chart showing ImageNet top-1 accuracy for five models.

The x-axis is labeled Model and lists five categories: ResNet-50, ViT-B/16, ConvNeXt-T, Swin-T, and Ours. The y-axis is labeled Top-1 accuracy (%) and runs from 70 to 88, in 2-point steps; it does not start at zero.

There is one panel and one series of bars, with no legend. The categories are the five model names just listed.

The bar values are 76.1 for ResNet-50, 81.8 for ViT-B/16, 82.1 for ConvNeXt-T, 81.3 for Swin-T, and 84.6 for Ours. The lowest value is ResNet-50 at 76.1, and the highest is Ours at 84.6.

The main pattern is that all four newer models are above ResNet-50 by about 5 to 9 points. Among the non-Ours models, ConvNeXt-T is slightly highest at 82.1, ViT-B/16 is close at 81.8, and Swin-T is a little lower at 81.3. Ours is the clear top performer, about 2.5 points above ConvNeXt-T and about 8.5 points above ResNet-50.

This is a grouped bar chart showing benchmark scores for three model sizes across three benchmarks.

The x-axis is labeled Benchmark and has three categories: GLUE, SuperGLUE, and SQuAD F1. The y-axis is labeled Score and runs from 50 to 100, in increments of 10; it does not start at zero. There is one panel.

The legend is titled Model size, with three series: Small, Base, and Large.

For GLUE, Small is about 78, Base about 84, and Large about 89. For SuperGLUE, Small is about 65, Base about 71, and Large about 79. For SQuAD F1, Small is about 83, Base about 88.5, and Large about 91.

The main pattern is that scores rise consistently as model size increases for every benchmark. SQuAD F1 is highest overall, GLUE is next, and SuperGLUE is lowest for all three model sizes. The largest gap appears on SuperGLUE, where Large is about 14 points above Small.

This is a confusion matrix heatmap showing how often four classes were predicted correctly or confused with each other on the test set.

The x-axis is Predicted label and the y-axis is True label. Both axes list the categories cat, dog, bird, and car. There is one panel, and the color scale on the right runs from 0 up to about 100, with darker blue meaning higher counts. The chart does not use logarithmic axes.

The series or groups are the four class labels cat, dog, bird, and car, arranged as rows and columns of the matrix.

The diagonal values are 88 for cat, 84 for dog, 90 for bird, and 97 for car. Off-diagonal values are cat misread as dog 9, bird 2, car 1; dog misread as cat 11, bird 3, car 2; bird misread as cat 3, dog 4, car 3; and car misread as cat 0, dog 1, bird 2. The largest single value is 97 for true car predicted as car, and the smallest is 0 for true car predicted as cat.

The main pattern is that most counts are on the diagonal, so classification is generally strong. Car is the best recognized class, followed by bird, cat, and dog. The most notable confusions are between cat and dog, especially dog predicted as cat at 11 and cat predicted as dog at 9.

This is a heatmap showing attention strengths from one transformer head, with query tokens on the vertical axis and key tokens on the horizontal axis.

The x-axis is labeled Key token and the y-axis is labeled Query token. Both axes list the tokens The, cat, sat, on, the, mat, and a period. The color scale runs from 0.0 to 1.0, with darker purple meaning lower attention and yellow meaning higher attention. There is one panel.

There is no legend beyond the token labels and the colorbar. The highlighted cells are on the diagonal and a few off-diagonal positions.

The largest value is at query The attending to key The, at 1.0. Query cat to key cat is about 0.9. Query sat to key sat is about 0.8. Query on to key on is about 0.8. The second the, at query the and key the, is about 0.75. Query mat to key mat is about 0.4 to 0.5. Query period to key period is about 0.65. A noticeable off-diagonal value is query mat to key cat at about 0.5. Most other cells are near zero, roughly 0.0 to 0.1.

The main pattern is a strong mostly diagonal attention structure, meaning each token mostly attends to itself or nearby earlier tokens, with especially strong attention on The, cat, sat, and on. The mat row is the most spread out, with a clear extra focus on cat. The period row is moderate and fairly distributed, while the rest of the matrix is very dark and low.

This is a scatter plot showing MMLU accuracy versus parameter count for three model families.

The x-axis is labeled Parameters, in billions, and runs from about 5 to 70; it does not start at zero. The y-axis is labeled MMLU, in percent, and runs from about 55 to 88; it also does not start at zero. There is one panel.

The legend is titled Family, with three series: Dense in blue circles, MoE in orange x marks, and Distilled in green squares.

The main visible points are: Dense starts at about 56.5 percent at 6 billion and about 59 percent at 8 billion, then rises through about 64 at 12 billion, 70 at 20 billion, 71 at 23 billion, 74 at 31 billion, 76 at 34 billion, 78.5 at 44 billion, 81 at 47 billion, 81.7 at 50 billion, 80.6 at 59 billion, 87 at 65 billion, and about 84.7 at 68 billion. MoE starts at about 56 at 6 billion and 59 at 8 billion, then about 64.7 at 10 billion, 75 at 22 billion, 75 at 27 billion, 78.5 at 30 billion, 79 at 33 billion, 80.5 at 36 billion, 82.5 at 40 billion, 85 at 52 billion, 83 at 55 billion, 84.5 at 58 billion, 84.5 at 59 billion, and about 86.8 at 66 billion. Distilled starts at about 61 at 11 billion, 62 at 14 billion, 68.5 at 19 billion, 69.7 at 20 billion, 71.8 at 27 billion, 72.8 at 30 billion, 73.8 at 37 billion, 74.5 at 41 billion, 74.2 at 43 billion, 77.7 at 47 billion, 80.7 at 65 billion, and 78 at 68 billion.

The overall pattern is that MMLU increases with parameter count for all three families. MoE is usually highest, Dense is generally in the middle, and Distilled is usually lowest. The highest point is about 87 percent for Dense around 65 billion parameters, and the lowest points are around 56 percent at about 6 billion parameters.

This is a box-and-whisker plot showing inference latency for four kinds of hardware.

The x-axis is Hardware with four categories: CPU, GPU, TPU, and Edge NPU. The y-axis is Latency in milliseconds, ranging from about 0 up to a little over 190, and it is a linear scale that does not start at zero on the visible plotting area, though zero is shown at the bottom.

There is one panel. The four groups are CPU, GPU, TPU, and Edge NPU.

For CPU, the median is about 116 ms, the box runs from about 106 to 141 ms, and the whiskers extend from about 68 to 188 ms. For GPU, the median is about 17 ms, the box is about 14 to 20 ms, and the whiskers are about 10 to 27 ms with one high outlier near 29 ms. For TPU, the median is about 11 ms, the box is about 9 to 13 ms, and the whiskers are about 7 to 20 ms with outliers around 22 to 24 ms. For Edge NPU, the median is about 43 ms, the box is about 37 to 48 ms, the whiskers are about 24 to 62 ms, and there are several high outliers around 65, 68, 72, 75, and 87 ms.

The main pattern is that CPU is by far the slowest, TPU is the fastest, GPU is slightly slower than TPU, and Edge NPU is in between but with several high outliers.

This is a split violin chart showing the distribution of score for three tasks, comparing results without chain-of-thought prompting and with chain-of-thought prompting.

The x-axis is Task, with three categories: Math, Code, and Writing. The y-axis is Score, with visible ticks at about 20, 40, 60, 80, and 100; it does not start at zero. There is one panel.

The legend is titled Condition, with two series: Without CoT in blue and With CoT in orange.

For Math, Without CoT is centered around the mid-50s, with dashed quartile lines at about 48, 56, and 62; With CoT is centered higher, around the mid-70s, with quartiles about 66, 74, and 79. For Code, Without CoT is around the low-to-mid 50s, with quartiles about 49, 55, and 62; With CoT is around the low 60s, with quartiles about 58, 64, and 70. For Writing, Without CoT is around the low-to-mid 50s, with quartiles about 48, 55, and 61; With CoT is around the mid-50s to low 60s, with quartiles about 48, 56, and 64. The overall ranges reach roughly from the low 30s up to about 100.

The main pattern is that With CoT is higher than Without CoT for Math and Code, especially Math, while Writing shows a smaller difference. Math with CoT has the highest scores, and the no-CoT groups cluster in the mid-50s across all three tasks.

This is an overlaid histogram with smooth density curves showing the distribution of logit margins for two groups, in-distribution and out-of-distribution.

The x-axis is labeled Logit margin and runs from about minus 3.5 to 5, with evenly spaced linear ticks; it does not start at zero. The y-axis is labeled Count and runs from 0 up to about 185. There is one panel. The title is Distribution of logit margins.

The legend is titled Split and has two series: In-distribution in blue and Out-of-distribution in orange.

The blue in-distribution histogram peaks just below 0, around minus 0.2 to 0.0, with a highest bar near 175 counts and the smooth curve peaking around 155 to 160. It spans roughly from minus 3 to about 3, with most mass between about minus 1.5 and 1.5. The orange out-of-distribution histogram peaks around 3.0 to 3.2, with a highest bar around 120 to 135 counts and a curve peak around 130 to 135. It spans roughly from about 1.5 to 4.6, with most mass between about 2.2 and 3.8.

The main pattern is that the two distributions are clearly separated: in-distribution values are centered near zero and slightly negative, while out-of-distribution values are shifted far to the right. There is only a small overlap around about 2 to 2.5, and the orange group is more concentrated than the blue group.

This is a scatter plot with a fitted line that shows a strong positive relationship between GPU hours and throughput in tokens per second.

The x-axis is labeled GPU hours, in thousands, and runs from about 0 to 10. The y-axis is labeled Tokens/s, in thousands, and runs from about 2 to 27. Neither axis is logarithmic, and both start slightly above zero on the visible plot area rather than exactly at zero.

There is one series of blue circular points, plus a blue regression line with a lightly shaded confidence band. The title says Compute vs. throughput with r = 0.94.

The lowest points are around 2 to 3 thousand tokens per second at about 0.5 GPU hours. The highest point is about 26 thousand tokens per second at around 8.5 GPU hours. The fitted line starts near 5 thousand tokens per second at x equals 0 and rises to about 25 thousand at x equals 10. Around 5 GPU hours, the points are mostly between about 12 and 20 thousand tokens per second. Around 8 to 10 GPU hours, they are mostly between about 19 and 26 thousand.

The main pattern is a clear upward trend: more GPU hours correspond to higher throughput. The points are fairly tightly clustered around the line, which matches the high correlation. There are a few outliers, including one low point near 2.5 thousand tokens per second and a few points above the line around 12 to 16 thousand tokens per second at low to middle x values.

This is a line chart showing how test error changes as dataset size increases for three optimizers.

The x-axis is labeled “Dataset size (tokens)” and is logarithmic, with ticks at about 10 to the 6, 10 to the 7, 10 to the 8, 10 to the 9, and 10 to the 10 tokens. The y-axis is labeled “Error” and runs from about 0.8 up to a little over 3.0; it does not start at zero. There is one panel.

The legend is titled “Optimizer” and includes three series: SGD in blue, Adam in orange, and Muon in green.

At 10 to the 6 tokens, all three start at about 3.0 error. At 3 million tokens, SGD is about 2.7, Adam about 2.65, and Muon about 2.6. At 10 million, SGD is about 2.42, Adam about 2.30, and Muon about 2.28. At 30 million, SGD is about 2.27, Adam about 2.07, and Muon about 1.95. At 100 million, SGD is about 1.98, Adam about 1.89, and Muon about 1.70. At 300 million, SGD is about 1.78, Adam about 1.66, and Muon about 1.45. At 1 billion, SGD is about 1.62, Adam about 1.45, and Muon about 1.27. At 3 billion, SGD is about 1.50, Adam about 1.28, and Muon about 1.06. At 10 billion, SGD is about 1.34, Adam about 1.15, and Muon about 0.91.

All three lines slope downward as data increases, and Muon is lowest after the smallest sizes, Adam is in the middle, and SGD is highest. The gap between them widens at larger dataset sizes.

This is a two-panel line chart showing model accuracy over epochs and a learning-rate sweep of final validation accuracy.

The left panel, labeled “(a) Accuracy,” has Epoch on the x-axis from 0 to 30 and Accuracy on the y-axis from about 0.25 to 1.0; it is not logarithmic. The right panel, labeled “(b) Learning-rate sweep,” has Learning rate on the x-axis on a logarithmic scale from 10 to the minus 4 to 10 to the minus 2, and Final validation accuracy on the y-axis from about 0.62 to 0.90.

The legend in the left panel has two series: Train in blue and Validation in orange. The right panel has one blue series with square markers and no separate legend.

In the accuracy panel, training accuracy starts at about 0.27 and rises to about 0.91 by epoch 12, then climbs to about 0.995 by epoch 30. Validation accuracy starts at about 0.27, reaches about 0.91 at epoch 12, peaks around 0.94 to 0.95 near epochs 16 to 18, and ends around 0.87 at epoch 30.

In the learning-rate panel, the points are about 0.81 at 10 to the minus 4, 0.86 at 3 times 10 to the minus 4, 0.888 at 10 to the minus 3, 0.84 at 3 times 10 to the minus 3, and 0.62 at 10 to the minus 2.

The main pattern is that training keeps improving steadily, while validation improves then slightly declines, suggesting overfitting after the middle epochs. In the sweep, performance peaks near 10 to the minus 3 and drops sharply at the largest learning rate.

This is a three-panel line chart showing accuracy over training epochs for three datasets, comparing two augmentation settings.

The x-axis in each panel is Epoch, from 0 to 100. The y-axis is Accuracy, shown from about 0 to 0.9, and it does not start at zero because the lower edge is slightly below 0. There are three panels: CIFAR-10 on the left, CIFAR-100 in the middle, and Tiny-ImageNet on the right.

The legend on the right is titled Augmentation, with two series: None in blue and RandAugment in orange.

For CIFAR-10, both lines start at 0.0, rise to about 0.58 at 20 epochs, about 0.74 to 0.76 at 30, about 0.85 to 0.87 at 50, and end around 0.90 for None and about 0.93 for RandAugment at 100. For CIFAR-100, they start at 0.0, reach about 0.45 to 0.47 at 20, about 0.61 to 0.64 at 40, and end around 0.69 for None and 0.74 for RandAugment. For Tiny-ImageNet, they start at 0.0, reach about 0.35 to 0.38 at 20, about 0.47 to 0.53 at 40, and end around 0.55 for None and 0.60 for RandAugment.

The main pattern is that accuracy rises quickly early, then levels off. RandAugment is consistently above None in all three panels, with the biggest gap on Tiny-ImageNet and the smallest gap on CIFAR-10.

This is a dot-and-error-bar chart showing the mean BLEU score with standard deviation over 5 seeds for four model variants.

The x-axis is labeled Variant and has four categories: Full model, minus attention, minus residual, and minus norm. The y-axis is labeled BLEU, with values shown from about 56 to about 73. The axis is linear and does not start at zero.

There is one panel and four groups, one for each variant.

The Full model is at about 71.5 BLEU, with error bars from about 70.3 to 72.8. Minus attention is about 65.3, with error bars from about 64.3 to 66.4. Minus residual is about 56.6, with very small error bars from about 56.3 to 56.9. Minus norm is about 66.6, with error bars from about 65.0 to 68.2.

The main pattern is that the Full model is highest. Removing residual hurts performance the most and is by far the lowest. Removing attention also lowers BLEU a lot, while removing norm lowers it less than removing attention but still clearly below the full model.

This is a scatterplot matrix with smooth density curves on the diagonal, showing how petal length, petal width, and sepal length vary by species group.

The matrix has three variables on both axes: petal length, petal width, and sepal length. The x and y axes are in plain numeric units, not logarithmic, and they do not all start at zero. Petal length is shown roughly from about 1.0 to 6.5, petal width from about 0.0 to 2.5, and sepal length from about 4.0 to 7.5. There are nine panels total, one for each pairwise combination, with the three diagonal panels showing distributions for each variable.

The legend has three groups: setosa-like in blue, versicolor-like in orange, and virginica-like in green.

The blue group is around petal length 1 to 2, petal width 0 to 0.5, and sepal length about 4.3 to 5.8. The orange group is around petal length 3.8 to 5.0, petal width about 1.0 to 1.5, and sepal length about 5.0 to 7.1. The green group is around petal length 4.7 to 6.3, petal width about 1.6 to 2.3, and sepal length about 6.0 to 7.4.

The main pattern is clear separation by species, especially in petal length and petal width. Blue points are lowest, orange are in the middle, and green are highest. Sepal length overlaps more, but green is generally longest, blue shortest, and orange in between.

This is a clustered heatmap showing normalized task scores for five methods across six tasks, with dendrograms clustering both the rows and the columns.

The x-axis lists the tasks Trans., Code, Math, Summ., QA, and NLI, with no units shown. The y-axis lists the methods M3, M4, M2, M1, and M5. The color scale at upper left runs from 0.5 to 1.0, with blue for lower values and red for higher values. There is one main panel.

The row groups are M3, M4, M2, M1, and M5. The column groups are Trans., Code, Math, Summ., QA, and NLI.

The highest visible values are around 1.0 for M3 on Code and about 0.9 for M3 on Math. M3 is also about 0.8 on Trans. and about 0.7 on Summ., but about 0.5 on QA and NLI. M4 is about 0.6 on Trans., about 0.85 on Code and Math, about 0.55 on Summ., about 0.45 on QA, and about 0.3 on NLI. M2 is about 0.3 on Trans., about 0.35 to 0.4 on Code and Math, about 0.55 on Summ., about 0.75 on QA, and about 0.45 on NLI. M1 is about 0.4 on Trans., about 0.25 on Code, about 0.3 on Math, about 0.85 on Summ., about 0.65 on QA, and about 0.7 on NLI. M5 is about 0.35 on Trans., about 0.2 on Code, about 0.3 on Math, about 0.75 on Summ., about 0.7 on QA, and about 0.75 on NLI.

The main pattern is that M3 and M4 cluster together and score best on Code and Math, while M1 and M5 cluster together and score best on Summ., QA, and NLI. M2 sits between these groups, doing relatively better on QA. Trans. is moderate for M3 and M4, but lower for the others.

This is a two-line cumulative distribution chart showing the proportion of responses at or below each response length for two decoding methods.

The x-axis is labeled Tokens generated, ranging from about 0 to 1600, and it is linear. The y-axis is labeled Proportion, ranging from 0 to 1.0, and it is linear; it does not start below zero. There is one panel.

The legend is titled Decoding and has two series: Greedy in blue and Speculative in orange.

For Speculative, the curve rises very quickly: it is about 0.2 at 50 tokens, about 0.5 at 100, about 0.8 at 175 to 200, about 0.95 at 300, and reaches about 1.0 by around 450 tokens. For Greedy, it is about 0.1 at 50 tokens, about 0.2 at 100, about 0.4 at 200, about 0.6 at 300, about 0.75 at 400, about 0.9 at 550, about 0.95 at 650, and approaches 1.0 only near 1000 tokens and above.

The main pattern is that Speculative responses are consistently shorter than Greedy responses: its curve is much farther left, meaning a given proportion is reached at far fewer tokens. Greedy has a much longer tail, extending out to around 1600 tokens, while Speculative is nearly saturated by about 450 tokens.

This is a horizontal bar chart showing how many papers are in the survey for each conference venue.

The x-axis is labeled count and runs from 0 to a little over 400, with regular tick marks every 50; it is linear and starts at zero. The y-axis is labeled Venue and lists six categories: NeurIPS, ICML, ICLR, ACL, CVPR, and EMNLP.

There is one panel, and each bar corresponds to one venue.

The counts are approximately 415 for NeurIPS, 305 for ICML, 375 for ICLR, 155 for ACL, 290 for CVPR, and 135 for EMNLP.

The main pattern is that NeurIPS is the largest by a clear margin, ICLR is second, ICML and CVPR are in the middle, and ACL and especially EMNLP are much smaller. The bars are not close to each other except for ICML and CVPR, which are fairly similar.
